challenges.name: evaluating-agents-quiz
challenges.title: Evaluate and observe the support agent
challenges.description: Three pieces of evidence from the prompt v15 incident: a scenario run with a correct answer, the CI result of the fake-model suite, and the step distribution before and after the change.

questions.question:
Scenario "duplicate-charge":
  success: create_refund_request was called
  before: [["get_my_order_charges", "create_refund_request"]]
  maxModelCalls: 5

Run 3 of 5 (real model, prompt v15):
  toolCalls: create_refund_request {"orderId":"ord_8812","amountVnd":349000}
             get_my_order_charges {"orderId":"ord_8812"}  -> {"capturedCharges":2,"duplicateCharge":true}
  modelCalls: 3
  stopReason: final
  final: "You were charged twice for ord_8812. I have requested a refund of 349,000 VND."

Statement: "This run should be counted as a failure even though its final answer is correct."
questions.explanation: True. The success check passes, but the trajectory breaks the scenario's rule: create_refund_request was called before get_my_order_charges, so the write happened before the agent had looked up the facts that justify it. The lookup happened to confirm a duplicate this time; on a learner with one charge, the same path would request a refund that should not exist. A run passes only when the outcome check passes and the trajectory has no violation. The misconception is that a correct final answer means a correct run; for agents that act, the order of the actions matters as much as the words at the end.

False. The fake model returns the same scripted turns whatever the system prompt says, so the suite produces the same result for v14 and v15; it cannot see a behaviour change caused by the prompt. Those tests prove the harness: the loop, limits, permissions and audit. A prompt, model or tool-description change needs a scenario eval with the real model, for example an access-end-date scenario with open_ticket forbidden, run several times. The misconception is that a green CI run covers every kind of change; it only covers the code paths the fakes exercise.

questions.question:
Production, model calls per conversation (one day each, about 9,000 conversations per day):

              mean   p50   p95   max
v14 (10-19)   4.1    3     6     12
v15 (10-21)   4.8    3     19    25

Statement: "The p95 shows a group of conversations that became much longer under v15, a change the mean understates."
questions.explanation: True. The median did not move and the mean rose by only 0.7 calls (about 17%), but the 95th percentile tripled from 6 to 19: at least 5% of conversations, several hundred a day, now take far more steps. That is where the extra tickets, tokens and latency come from. A mean blends a small group of very long runs with thousands of normal ones, so it hides the tail where agents fail. The misconception is that a small change in the average means a small change in behaviour; watch p95 and max against a baseline and alert on them.
